Meditation

Meditation is a simple and powerful practice that switches off the stress state of your brain and body and focuses your thoughts in a calm and productive way.

Neural Networks That Fire Together, Wire Together

The brain’s fight-flight response system kicks in when we feel we are in danger or perceive a threat. It’s what makes us feel uncomfortable and anxious and can disrupt our ability to manage stress, concentrate, and engage in positive social interactions.

Meditation activates and strengthens your brain’s reward networks that are involved in your awareness of positive experiences.

Practicing meditation regularly can help you become aware of negative thinking traps and strengthen brain networks involved in being focused and attentive in the moment. Remember: neural networks that fire together, wire together.

Just a few days of mindfulness meditation training has been shown to increase functional coupling between the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and the default mode network (DMN) in the posterior cingulate cortex. This coupling is believed to reflect greater top-down executive control at rest, and this network is also involved in maintaining attention and focus 1.

Scientific randomized controlled trials have shown benefits of mindfulness meditation training for a range of psychological and other health conditions, including reduced stress, anxiety, depression, heart rate, and blood pressure. 

These brain-based meditations will teach you to enhance your calmness and be in the moment, to be self-reflective in a non-judgmental way, and to direct your subconscious mind to be more tuned in to the positive things around you.

Mindfulness meditation has been directly shown to decrease activity in the amygdala, a key brain structure involved in heightened vigilance and alertness to potential danger . 

Practicing simple mindfulness exercises during your normal daily routine call help your brain learn to reduce negativity and focus better. 


An easy way to do this is to focus on the sensory environment around you. You can practice during a range of daily routines - while you are walking along the street, making morning coffee and breakfast, or even taking a shower. 

Welcome all sounds and be open to explore them with a child’s curiosity. This simple practice induces your calm “in the moment” response and allows your brain to stop being caught up in the typical flow of overwhelming thoughts, worries and to-do lists. Focusing on your senses is a quick and simple way to become present. happening right now. 


This can be done in-the-moment to bring focus to your task at hand, or can be done as a daily routine practice to bring calmness and focus to your normal state of mind, which also puts you in a stronger frame of mind to deal with stress and challenges when they do arise.

NeuroTunes

NeuroTunes is a neuroscience-based music and soundscapes tool to reduce anxiety and stress in-the-moment. Music can generate different brain states by driving the brain's highly interconnected neural networks to fire in time to the music, through a mechanism known as "entrainment". Music specifically designed to modify the brain and body state

The individual building blocks of music—including tempo, rhythm, melody, pitch, and harmony—can be designed to create music that calms the mind and relaxes the body. When music is simpler and more predictable, the brain is lulled into a state of calm and relaxation. By contrast, complex and bombastic arrangements can produce a sense of unease and anxiety (Crusius, 2018). There is also a "Binaural Beat" additional entrainment boost to enhance calm, which is embedded in some of the sounds and music (Huang & Charyton, 2008).

NeuroTunes build upon this foundation with soundscapes to soothe the mind and body with relaxed rhythms, legato phrasing, and minimal dynamic contrasts. 

The original composition tracks have been created with a precise tempo, and tempo variations, designed to lead listeners into a deep state of calm, and omitting specific musical elements that distract and reduce cognitive focus. 

Tracks additionally use 3D audio to create an optimally immersive experience. Listeners have the option to add sound waves and vibrations that promote slower frequency brainwaves that promote deeper states of relaxation, including binaural beats (beats transmitted separately to the two ears) and isochronic tones (tones turned on and off quickly). 

Music is one of the greatest ways to stimulate the brain. For example, when you provide an input to the brain to that one beat every two seconds, it particularly activates the main inhibitory, the calming chemical in the brain, you know, GABA.

When a sound enters the brain, it has a sort of cascade effect like dropping a pebble into water. And that cascade effect is called entrainment. And so, the sound you put in influences is the frequency that brainwaves are oscillating at.

Emotion state, positive to negative, is mainly driven by the pitch of the music. And arousal, how much your autonomic nervous system is activated or calmed down, is mainly driven by tempo of the music. 

NeuroTunes calming music is kept between 60 to 80 beats per minute, and the loudness is kept below  60 decibels. It is also kept simple and predictable, as this promotes calmness, and doesn’t stir up the brain too much.

The binaural beats within the music tracks are what really makes NeuroTunes unique. Binaural beats puts a different frequency of sound into each ear, which sort of brings the brain together, like a 3D visual effect but with music. And that brings the hemisphere synchronously working together better. The binaural beats are at around 10 cycles per second, which is the alpha frequency that is the calming frequency for the brain. 

Within the NeuroTunes tracks, there are also options to adjust the volume of the binaural beats and isochronic tones, to personalize it to your own liking.

The most effective way to go into a deep calm state is to calm heart rate. NeuroTunes slows down the tempo of the music over several minutes, at a frequency range close to resting heart rate, which is designed to slow down heart rate over the course of the music track. 

The instruments used have very little attack or dynamics to them. 

One of the unique approaches here is really diving deeper into the research and the papers and understanding how important the simplicity of this music has to be, but still keeping it interesting enough so that you can listen to it for six minutes.

 You know, you can habituate to a simple tone if it's just there forever, but the beauty of music is we can keep it entertaining. Feeling really good, but not over-excite you.  First is melody. If you have a melody that goes all over the place like somewhere over the rainbow, that’s not what you want to relax to. You want really simple one or two tones that are happening in the timeline. And those are slightly repetitive, but not completely repetitive. You want keys that are major and comfortable. You want dynamics that are within a certain range so that nothing is too loud at a certain part, or too soft, where people are reaching to hear it. You want it to be like a really comfortable, easy to lay on blanket for you to relax.

The general style this music is legato, slow, and smooth. So all the instrument selections, all the articulations, all the performances are done with that in mind.

Resonant Breathing



Designed to help increase Heart Rate Variability (HRV), this exercise involves breathing at 6 breaths per minute (or slower rates can also be selected), for a period of several minutes (with exact length chosen by user).

Heart rate variability is controlled by the Vagus nerve and parasympathetic nervous system, which is responsible for bodily responses of feeling safe and relaxed. This is in contrast to the sympathetic nervous system, which controls bodily responses to stress and avoiding danger - including higher heart rate, faster breathing, sweating more, as well as digestive system slowing and muscle tension. All of these responses are calmed down by the parasympathetic nervous system, which directly inhibits the sympathetic nervous system (Cacioppo et al., 2000).

The easiest part of these systems to influence and change is breathing. By breathing more slowly, it calms the sympathetic nervous system and boosts the parasympathetic nervous system activity instead. 

Low and High HRV

High Stress is strongly related to HRV.  This is true both for the immediate in-the-moment experience of stressful situations, as well as longer term presence of chronic life stressors. This has been established for day-to-day reporting of stress levels (Punita et al., 2016; Sin et al., 2016), and for work stress (both self-reported work experience (Chandola et al., 2008; Hinstanen et al., 2007) and objective ranking of work role responsibilities and expectations (Kang et al., 2004)). Similarly, lower HRV is related to emotional brain system disruptions in clinical disorders, including depression and anxiety (Thayer et al., 1996; Chalmers et al., 2014; Williams et al., 2015; Carney et al., 2001; Agelink et al., 2002; Hartmann et al., 2019), PTSD (Cohen et al., 1997), and cravings in substance use disorders (Culbertson et al., 2010; Moon et al., 2023).

Conversely, increased Heart Rate Variability is also associated with better cognitive and emotional functioning, including Memory (Frewen et al., 2013; Thayer 2003; Hansen et al., 2009), Focus and Attention (Hansen et al.,, 2003, 2009; Frewen et al., 2013; Zeki Al Hazzouri et al., 2017; Williams et al., 2016), Flexibility and Planning (Colzato et al., 2018 ; Ottaviani et al.,  2019), Visuospatial Skills (Frewen et al.,  2013), Impulsivity Control (Hansen et al., 2009), better Resilience (Williams et al., 2015 ; Nasso et al., 2019), greater compassion and more positive social interactions (Lischke et al., 2018 ; Rockliff et al., 2008 ; Shahrestani et al., 2015) and better sleep and recovery (Arslan et al., 2019 ; Gouin et al., 2013). 

Resonant Breathing Training

Resonant breathing training at around 6 breaths per minute has been demonstrated to reduce sympathetic nervous system activity (Szulczewski & Rynkiewicz, 2018), and to increase HRV and lower cortisol levels and reported stress and anxiety shortly after breathing practice (Dawson et al., 2014 ; Fuchs et al., 2018; Wells et al., 2012).

In a 2024 meta-analysis of 31 studies (N=1133; 9 RCTs), HRV was found to be significantly increased with a moderate to large effect size immediately following resonant breathing practice (RMSSD, SDNN from 10 studies, with larger effect sizes in the RCT studies), along with significantly lowered systolic blood pressure and moderate evidence of reduced perceived negative emotion. Additionally, reductions in negative emotion immediately following resonant breathing were found to correlate with the degree of HRV increase achieved (from 5 studies; Shao et al., 2024).

In a 2024 meta-analysis of 31 studies (N=1133; 9 RCTs), HRV was found to be significantly increased with a moderate to large effect size immediately following resonant breathing practice (RMSSD, SDNN from 10 studies, with larger effect sizes in the RCT studies), along with significantly lowered systolic blood pressure and moderate evidence of reduced perceived negative emotion. Additionally, reductions in negative emotion immediately following resonant breathing were found to correlate with the degree of HRV increase achieved (from 5 studies; Shao et al., 2024). 

The existing reviews suggested that slow-paced breathing improves cardiovascular functions such as increasing HRV (Zaccaro et al., 2018)

Sustained resonant breathing practice over several days to weeks has been found to significantly lower blood pressure, stress, anxiety and depression (Berry et al., 2014 ; Jester et al., 2019 ; Lee et al., 2015 ; Paul & Garg, 2012 ; Serafim et al., 2019; Shao et al., 2024), and to improve sleep quality (Tsai et al., 2015). Conversely, short rapid breathing, such as occurs during states of stress and anxiety, itself has been shown to further activate the sympathetic nervous system (Leung et al., 2006).

Resonant breathing training has also been found to improve cognitive focus and control, executive function, learning and decision-making performance - both in-the-moment after several minutes of training, and also after several weeks of ongoing regular practice (De Couck et al., 2019 ; Hoffman et al., 2019 ; Laborde et al., 2019, 2021; Paul et al., 2012).

In addiction, resonant breathing training has been found to reduce cravings for alcohol, nicotine, drugs and food. As with mood and cognition, this effect has been seen both immediately following breathing exercises, and with sustained practice over a period of several weeks (Eddie et al., 2014 ; McLernon et al., 2004 ; Meule et al., 2012 ; Penzlin et al., 2015). 

Mechanisms of Action and Neuroplasticity

The main function of the Vagus nerve is to suppress the body’s fight-flight system, which is triggered in response to stress; enabling the stress response to end and recovery to begin. The Vagus nerve serves as the body's superhighway, carrying information between the brain and the internal organs and controlling the body's response in times of rest and relaxation – including gut function, inflammation, facial expressions, tone of voice, heart rate and heart rate variability. Stress responses in all of these systems are calmed down by parasympathetic nervous system activity (Cacioppo et al., 2000).

The brain systems that create and maintain a stress response also change depending on this feedback from the body. 

Ongoing stress responses from the body serve to maintain and strengthen an upward spiral of stress and vigilance network activity within the brain. Conversely, activity from the parasympathetic nervous system serves to calm down not only bodily responses, but the emotional brain networks that are maintaining a heightened state of distress and unease.

Most of the time, the Vagus nerve and parasympathetic system should be more dominant, and heart rate variability should be high. However, when there are ongoing states of high stress, the fight-flight sympathetic nervous system can become more dominant on a longer term and more chronic basis. 

There are three physiological sources that contribute to Heart Rate Variability:

Respiration (Respiratory Sinus Arrythmia, or RSA)

Blood Pressure (the Baroreflex)

Rhythm in Vascular Tone

The resonant frequency breathing rate is the only rate at which respiration and blood pressure are synchronized, which makes it the ideal breathing rate for calming bodily responses associated with stress. 

Heart rate changes as you breathe – increasing during inhalation and decreasing during exhalation (see Figure 2). During inhalation, activity of the vagus nerve is suppressed, causing at automatic increase in the sympathetic nervous system connections to the heart, which causes heart rate to increase. Whereas during exhalation, the vagus nerve innervation within the brainstem is once again restored and heart rate consequently decreases (Lehrer & Gevirtz, 2014 ; Sevoz-Couche & Laborde, 2022). This means that even though heart rate and respiration changes are coupled, there is a short delay with heart rate following respiration changes.

RSA (Respiratory Sinus Arrythmia) amplitude is the difference between the high-point peak and low-point trough of heart rate values as you breathe in and out, with the greatest variability in heart rate being achieved at the highest RSA amplitude.

Whereas during exhalation, the vagus nerve innervation within the brainstem is once again restored and heart rate consequently decreases (Lehrer & Gevirtz, 2014 ; Sevoz-Couche & Laborde, 2022). This means that even though heart rate and respiration changes are coupled, there is a short delay with heart rate following respiration changes.

RSA (Respiratory Sinus Arrythmia) amplitude is the difference between the high-point peak and low-point trough of heart rate values as you breathe in and out, with the greatest variability in heart rate being achieved at the highest RSA amplitude. Resonant Breathing is the slow breathing rate which creates the maximal RSA amplitude (i.e. the greatest difference between the maximum and minimum heart rate levels). For most people, this is around 6 breaths a minute for women and around 5.5 breaths a minute for men (Song & Lehrer, 2003 ; Vaschillo et al. 2002). Breathing at other slow breathing rates between normal breathing and around 6 breaths per minute increasing improves RSA amplitude, however no additional benefit is gained by breathing slower than the resonant frequency rate (Hirsch & Bishop, 1981). RSA is controlled entirely by the vagus nerve and parasympathetic nervous system (Lehrer & Gevirtz, 2014).

Breathing at around 6 breaths a minute causes the amplitude of heart rate oscillations to grow to many times the amplitude at rest, while the overall pattern becomes simpler and more sinusoidal (Lehrer & Gevirtz, 2014; see Figure 2). There are several physiological processes happening at the same time contributing to this, including this being the only breathing rate at which heart rate oscillations are in phase with both breathing rate and blood pressure oscillations (Lehrer & Gevirtz, 2014).

Only at the resonance frequency of around 6 breaths per minute does this time-locked coherence of breathing, heart rate RSA (Respiratory Sinus Arrythmia) oscillations and blood pressure occur. This coherence causes all of these rhythms to reinforce each other, thus providing the optimal conditions for improving both heart rate variability and baroreflex sensitivity, and for feedback to brain networks for emotion regulation (Lehrer and Gevirtz, 2014; Sevoz-Couche & Laborde, 2022). 



Information for Clients and Providers about this Training Tool

Heart Rate Variability (HRV) is simply the beat-to-beat variation in a person’s heartbeat - the time difference between each consecutive beat. We want to have variability between our heartbeats.  Variability is the key to adaptive effectiveness.

HRV is controlled by the Vagus nerve and the parasympathetic nervous system, which is responsible for bodily responses of feeling safe and relaxed. This is contrast to the sympathetic nervous system, which controls bodily responses to stress and avoiding danger.

Heart Rate Variability (HRV) can be increased by training several minutes a day, breathing at 6 breaths per minute or less, with the Resonant Breathing exercise. Breathing at 6 breaths per minute, strengthens the blood pressure reflex (called the baroreflex) and sends messages to the brain via the Vagus nerve to increase Heart Rate Variability.

Most people breathe at 12 breaths a minute.  Breathing at 6 breaths per minute rapidly puts a brake on the fight-flight stress system and increases the Vagus system flexibility to adapt effectively to any task or situation. 

Increased Heart Rate Variability is linked to low stress, better wellness, better sleep and recovery, good cognitive flexibility and enhanced peak performance. Slow breathing training at 6 breaths per minute has been shown to improve sleep quality (Tsai et al., 2015), and to reduce sympathetic nervous system activity (Szulczewski & Rynkiewicz, 2018).

Resonant Breathing reduces stress and improves focus in all situations, by directly controlling the body’s automatic responses and calming them down

Stress

Stress occurs when your negative unconscious thoughts are greater than your capacity to consciously cope with them effectively.



Stress results from an ongoing state of high autonomic arousal, related to difficulty meeting the expectations or demands that are being made. When demands on us become more than we can meet, this is when stress coping becomes difficult and high stress results. 

At its core, your brain is wired to identify cues to avoid threat to keep you safe and identify possible rewards. This ongoing process is unconscious and occurs within a fifth of a second. It is the basis of your emotions, intuition and negative/positive biases that shape many of the approximately 50,000 thoughts you have every day. 

Not only can cues trigger stress, but just thinking about threat cues can trigger stress. 



These unconscious processes are modulated by slower more detailed conscious rational cognition, including memory, focus and planning that can over-ride these processes. 



Stress occurs when your negative unconscious thoughts are greater than your capacity to consciously cope with them effectively.

The “Stress Response” to any real or perceived threat induces a Fight-Flight response. 


Some stress is helpful, such as getting you out of immediate danger or to help you focus to complete a task. But when stress is overwhelmingly negative or continually triggered and becomes chronic, it derails performance.

On the opposite end of the spectrum is the “Relaxation Response”, which induces the Calm-Flexible system and helps you to cope effectively with the demands of your life.   

Daily life is an ongoing fluctuation and balance of your stress and calm response. 

Your effectiveness is increased by understanding what triggers stress for you and practicing the best techniques that put a brake on your stress response and boost your relaxation response.

5 Ways To Reframe Stress and Activate Your Relaxation Response



It is possible to reframe stress into awareness and compassion and find your best techniques to ‘turn on’ your relaxation response. 



Awareness and Compassion.



 It is important to be compassionate and understanding with yourself, and with others as well. 

You want to avoiding falling into the trap of thinking that there is ‘something wrong with you’ or beating yourself up about it. The important thing is to expect stressful challenges to arise, and to have some go-to strategies to help deal with it when they arise. 



Everyday Mindfulness.  

Re-train your brain to focus and stop unhelpful negative thoughts.



Practicing simple mindfulness exercises during your normal daily routine call help your brain learn to reduce negativity and focus better. 


An easy way to do this is to focus on the sensory environment around you. You can practice during a range of daily routines - while you are walking along the street, making morning coffee and breakfast, or even taking a shower. 

Welcome all sounds and be open to explore them with a child’s curiosity. This simple practice induces your calm “in the moment” response and allows your brain to stop being caught up in the typical flow of overwhelming thoughts, worries and to-do lists. Focusing on your senses is a quick and simple way to become present. happening right now. 


This can be done in-the-moment to bring focus to your task at hand, or can be done as a daily routine practice to bring calmness and focus to your normal state of mind, which also puts you in a stronger frame of mind to deal with stress and challenges when they do arise. 



Re-Train Your Brain To Notice The Positive And Fun Things.



Your brain is the ultimate danger detector. One of its most important functions is to keep you out of danger. But this is meant for a short-term heightened state of alertness until the potential danger passes, and you go back to feeling calm and safe again.



When everything you see and hear on the news and social media is telling your brain to be on constant high alert for danger, your threat-detection brain networks are constantly triggered to look for signs of danger more than normal. When danger signs are found it leads to more stress and reinforces the need to look for more danger. This creates a new brain state of heightened stress and worry that you can’t just shut off in a moment, even if the environment around you is no longer as dangerous as it was previously. 


You can train your brain back into a calmer and more positive state of being. One way is to purposely look out for and notice positive and fun things around you. 



Challenge yourself to pick out one positive thing each day that you consciously acknowledge – it could be as simple as seeing your neighbor’s dog go for a walk or noticing a fun moment with your family - and just acknowledging and focusing on that positive experience for a moment. 


By purposely noticing positive things you are consciously nudging the brain networks responsible for calmness and positivity to become more active. By looking out for things to reinforce positivity and calmness you can reduce the hyper-alert state of looking out for danger.

Repetition Of A Stimulus In The Moment. 



Dr Herbert Benson, a Harvard cardiologist, studied the significant body and brain changes of meditators and discovered something groundbreaking. Simply put: “ any repetition technique will break the train of everyday thought”. For example,  a repetition of slow breaths and saying a meaningful word to yourself as you exhale– or a repeating music sound or a repeating movement, will all generate significant calm. 



Benson also points to a way for each person to find what works best for them. Choose a word or mental association to create a deeper personal experience and induces authentic calm.
Mindfulness techniques, resonant breathing at 6 breaths a minute, and music compliment and can be carried into  movement practices, such as yoga, tai Chi and Chi Gong. Dr Herbert Benson discovered that repetition of any stimulus is the key to switch on your relaxation response, whether it is breath, meditation, a positive affirmation, a rhythmical sound, or movement (such as yoga or Tai chi).

You can take back control of your stress and worry systems by spending  a few minutes doing repetitive slow breathing. A constant negative news feed can hijack your internal systems of worry and stress,, now you can to do some hijacking yourself by tapping into the part of your brain’s worry network that is the easiest to control – your breath. By slow breathing for a few minutes, the brain-body feedback networks start to tell your brain that you are actually calm and safe, and this in turn reduces the upward cycle of stress and worry. This is again something that can be easy to fit into your daily routine. You can do this for a few minutes at your desk, while you are waiting for your children to do something, while you a sitting on the couch watching TV. 

This is an excellent in-the-moment method of calming yourself down. Practicing daily slow breathing, regardless of how you are feeling at that moment, is an effective way of calming down your baseline state of being and can lead you to feeling calmer, more focused and more productive when small daily stressors and challenges arise throughout the day. 



Repetition Of What Works For You Will Generate A New Habit. 

Working these techniques into your daily routine is key. Just 5-10 minutes day as a regular practice quickly becomes a daily built-in stress coping practice. Try out different types of exercises and then continue with the ones that work best you, and most importantly, that you will continue to include as a daily practice. The best stress reduction techniques are the ones that you are most likely to continue practicing on a regular basis. 

Any amount of stress reduction practice is helpful, but the more you continue to do the more benefit you will get.

A Brain-Based View of Stress “In the Moment”

At its core, your brain is wired to automatically identify cues to avoid threats to keep you safe and identify possible rewards. This ongoing process is unconscious and occurs within a fifth of a second.1  It is the basis of your emotions, intuition, and negative/positive biases that shape many of the approximately 50,000 thoughts you have every day. 


From your brain’s point of view, stress occurs when negative demands are greater than your capacity to consciously cope effectively. The gap between demand and capacity can be “acute” in the moment or can become “chronic” over time. This is considered an acute-chronic continuum. It is very well established that chronic stress is toxic to your body health, mental health, and performance. 


It is now becoming increasingly evident, that the sooner stress is stopped “in the moment”, the more effectively you will control the overall cascade of stress effects. Two lines of research that shed light on the importance of reducing stress in the moment, concern emotions and homeostasis.

Dr Lewis Coleman has recently elucidated the mechanism underlying the stress response. He highlights the importance of stopping any “over-reaction” to stress.2 Disruption of the micro-physiological details underlying any over-reaction to stress induces a cascade of negative impacts of stress and a loss of the fine tuning of the ongoing brain-body “homeostasis” (the brain-body’s healthy equilibrium). 

Emotional threats to our safety trigger the fight-flight stress response within a fifth of a second. Specific techniques in the moment can help activate the relaxation response and reduce the harmful effects of the stress toxicity cascade of microcellular processes. 



“The stress mechanism operates continuously, efficiently, and unobtrusively to repair tissues and regulate physiology, but like any mechanism, it has limitations. When its limits are exceeded, it wastes and depletes its substrates, generates harmful or defective excesses of its products, and produces a bewildering blizzard of destructive disease effects that disrupt physiology and damage organs and tissues.”3



The opposite end of the spectrum to The Stress Response is “The Relaxation Response,” which induces a calm, more flexible brain and associated body state. The Relaxation Response helps you to cope effectively with the demands of your life.   



Daily life is an ongoing fluctuation and balance between your stress and relaxation responses. Your effectiveness at managing stress is increased by understanding what emotion triggers your stress and how effectively you put a brake on your stress response and boost your relaxation response.

The impact that a high stress state has on you can be measured via your heartbeat patterns.  When you are in a high stress state you have a faster heart rate and lower variability between the heartbeats, than when you are in a calm relaxation response state (with lower rate and increased variability between beats). A relaxation response with high variability in consecutive heartbeats is the key to a healthy adaptive effectiveness, wellbeing, improved performance and a more resilient state of being.

Being in a state of high stress

leads to poorer eating habits. Higher stress

makes it harder to think clearly or focus,

reduces patience tolerance levels and the

ability to plan ahead and follow through

on that plan. In an additive effect to this,

the heightened negative emotion brain

state associated with stress leads us to

seek out “rewards” in our food choices,

and together, these influences lead to

selecting poorer food choices in times

of stress. The influence between stress

and food also goes back the other way,

with poor diet choices such as high sugar

content and fast foods leading to poorer

mental resources for stress coping. Sugar

creates a spike in blood sugar levels, which,

as they then rapidly fall, makes you irritable

and stress intolerant on the way back down. Inflammation can also occur due

to poor food choices, causing stress and

worsening existing stress. Mindful food

choices, a calm brain state, and slow eating

with presence and gratitude are powerful

antidotes to mitigate the unintended

consequences of sugar, oil, salt (SOS)

addictive eating.

Social connection and

social bonding directly impact stress, as

socially connecting with others releases

oxytocin, decreasing the stress hormone

cortisol. Being socially connected and

having a social support network can

play an important role in coping with

stress. Having a social support network

that is substantially smaller or poorer

quality than what you would like to have

is associated with higher stress and a

poorer ability to cope with that stress

level. Conversely, being highly satisfied

with the social connections and support

around you promotes better stress coping.

Exercise also has a synergistic effect on socialization, with any amount of

regular walking or other physical activity

being associated with higher energy and

socialization with others.

Sleep. Sleep and stress have a

bidirectional relationship. High levels of

stress lead to ongoing heightened brain

vigilance and thus, difficulty getting to

sleep. This is an effective mechanism to

keep us safe when a real physical threat is

close by but does not help us cope with

the types of stress that exist in modern

life. Poor sleep leads to much poorer

stress coping mechanisms due to reduced

emotional tolerance, increased irritability,

and poorer cognitive capacities for

focusing and planning. This bidirectional

relationship can easily lead to a spiraling of

increasing stress, poorer emotional coping,

and ongoing poor sleep. One way to break

this cycle is to practice resonant breathing,

listen to brain entrainment music, use

Alpha-Stim cranial electrotherapy

stimulation technology, and do a body scan relaxation before bed. Find what works for

you to reduce pre-sleep stress and induce

an optimal onset of sleep and better sleep

quality throughout the night.

Repetition of ANY Stimulus. Dr.

Herbert Benson discovered something

groundbreaking that can be applied to every

pillar of health. Put: “any repetition technique

will break the train of everyday thought.” For

example, a repetition of slow breaths, saying

a meaningful word or positive affirmation,

repeating musical sounds or repeating

yoga or tai chi movements, or chanting

in meditation all will generate a calming

relaxation response.

Induce presence by focusing on your breath

and senses. Use your surroundings to bring

your awareness to this moment. What do

you see, what do you hear? Ask yourself a

simple question, “Am I fully present?”

Your brain can primarily focus on one

thought at a time. Switching your focus to

your physical surroundings can induce calm

in your body. You can practice being present

during a range of daily routines - while you

are walking in nature or along the street,

making coffee, or just sitting at your desk. Pay

heightened attention to all sounds you can

hear around you for a short time. Welcome

all sounds without judgement and be open

to exploring them with a child’s curiosity. You

can do the same thing with what you can feel

or what you can smell.

Cognitive Behavior

Therapy (CBT)

techniques can also be

used to take control

of persistent negative

or worrying thoughts

that distract from other

tasks that you need to

focus on. One such

technique is to take one

minute to sit with the

distracting thought. You

can acknowledge that it

might be an important

issue causing problems

in your life, but also

then decide to put it to

one side for right this

moment (and visualize

doing so if you want to, so that the thought

sits beside you instead of between you and

the task you are completing), and decide

that you are choosing to put it to one side

for now and to focus on the task at hand in

this moment instead. It is still important to

think or talk through these thoughts and deal

with them at an appropriate time, but this

technique can be used for you to take back

control of when you address these thoughts

and not be hijacked in the moment by a

negative worry spiral in a way that you have

no control over. In this way, you can have a

Strategy for what you will do the next time a

worrying thought occurs to you.



Emotions give you a short cut to rapidly evaluate every interaction and situation in your life and determine if they are threatening or rewarding. 

Your brain’s emotion networks continually and rapidly scan for cues from your environment or people’s body language, that then quickly informs you of an impending threat or reward1. 

Emotions also drive your Stress Feelings.  Emotions and Feelings are different but directly complementary. Feelings are physical responses to emotions.  Emotions are the cause.  Feelings are the effect.  

Emotions trigger feelings and create a conscious awareness in your body, in the form of changes in heart rate, sweating, breathing and “gut’ activation. Stress is generated when “Emotion cue triggers” constantly pick up threat-cues in the environment and they hijack the brain into a stress response. This detection of threat could be a realistic evaluation of the surrounding environment, or it could also be that you are overly ‘tuned-in’ to detecting potential threat, and not paying attention to all the reward cues that are also around you. Stress is also generated when life’s demands exceed our capacity to cope. 

The stress response is a general alarm to deal with any perceived threat. It is helpful when in physical danger and to provide energy to enhance performance. But when stress is continually triggered, it becomes chronic and toxic to wellbeing, chronic illnesses, mental illness, and all performance. 

On the opposite end of the spectrum to the stress response, there is the Relaxation Response, which induces a Calm and Flexible brain and body state. Life is an ongoing fluctuation of Stress-Distress (Amygdala Fight-Flight reflex) and Calm-Flexible (Vagus nerve activated) states.

The good news is that there is a lot we can do trigger the Relaxation Response ourselves, to shift into a state that is calmer, healthier and more cognitively flexible and productive.
